entry.title: AutoGen Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Microsoft’s Multi-Agent Runtime

link.title: AutoGen Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Microsoft’s Multi-Agent Runtime

entry.content:
One agent with one while-loop is fine until the day your task needs a researcher, a coder, and a critic at the same time. Then you either cram all three personalities into one context window and hope, or you hand-roll threading code that breaks the first time an agent’s output has to become another agent’s input. The wall you hit is orchestration: who speaks next, who answers whom, when the whole thing has produced enough debate, and how to recover when one participant goes off the rails. A bare agent loop has no answer for any of that.

AutoGen, Microsoft’s open-source multi-agent framework, rebuilt itself in v0.4 around exactly this wall. Instead of shipping agent “recipes”, it ships primitives: agents are actors, a runtime routes every message, teams are group chats moderated by a dedicated manager agent, and stopping is a composable condition object rather than a hardcoded limit. Where LangChain composes steps into a graph and LlamaIndex leans data-first, AutoGen’s bet is that orchestration is fundamentally a message-passing problem — the same bet actor systems have made for decades.

This tour walks the source of autogen-core and autogen-agentchat to show how that bet pays off: an asyncio envelope queue, topic-based publish/subscribe, RPC futures, a group chat protocol with four selectable speaker policies, and a tool loop with reflection. By the end you’ll see how an event-driven runtime turns N chatting agents into a real orchestration engine.

AutoGen at a glance: AgentChat teams (top) register participants and a manager on the core runtime; every turn is routed as a message envelope; agents reply through model clients and tools until a termination condition fires and a TaskResult comes back.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The team is a driver, not a scheduler. run_stream, L351 starts an embedded runtime, registers participants plus a manager, and sends one GroupChatStart — the rest of the run is pure message flow.
  • One queue to route them all. SingleThreadedAgentRuntime, L149 keeps every RPC, publish and response as an envelope in a single asyncio queue (_message_queue, L257).
  • Two verbs, two semantics. send_message, L332 is point-to-point RPC returning a future; publish_message, L387 is fire-and-forget onto a topic.
  • Fan-out is subscription-based. _process_publish, L557 resolves subscribers for the topic, skips the sender, and asyncio.gathers delivery to all of them.
  • Subscriptions bind topics to agents. TypeSubscription, L10 maps a topic type onto an agent type; map_to_agent, L56 derives the exact AgentId from the topic’s source key.
  • Each chat agent wears an actor shell. ChatAgentContainer, L24 buffers the shared thread and, on handle_request, L86, calls the wrapped agent’s on_messages_stream.
  • The agent itself is model plumbing. AssistantAgent, L90 builds context and streams through the provider-agnostic ChatCompletionClient, L209 contract.
  • Memory plugs into the agent, not the runtime. update_context, L78 lets any Memory, L60 store inject retrieved content into the model context before a call.
  • Stopping is explicit. The manager applies a TerminationCondition, L15 after every turn; MaxMessageTermination, L62 is the simplest of a dozen composable stops.

The detail view: envelope dispatch and intervention on the left, the GroupChatStart → request → response protocol in the middle, four speaker-selection policies above, and AssistantAgent's tool loop with providers and tools below.

The Runtime Is a Message Bus with Actors

The core abstraction is the AgentRuntime, L21 protocol: send_message, publish_message, register_factory. Agents never call each other; they only address the runtime, which is what makes orchestration swappable — the in-process SingleThreadedAgentRuntime, L149 and a gRPC worker runtime in autogen-ext implement the same surface.

Dispatch is a pattern match. Both entry verbs stay thin — send_message and publish_message validate, serialize, and enqueue their envelope, then return immediately — while a host task started by start() drains the queue until stop_when_idle, L844 observes it empty, which is exactly how teams end a run. _process_next, L671 pulls one envelope and inspects its type: RPC envelopes go to _process_send, L466, publishes to _process_publish, L557, and responses to _process_response, L632, which finally resolves the future that send_message handed back to the original caller. Before any delivery, registered InterventionHandler, L20 hooks may rewrite or drop the message — a clean audit and guard rail seam.

Agents come in three flavors. BaseAgent, L60 is the abstract actor with a classmethod register that wraps a lazy factory (register_factory, L886, invoked on first contact by _invoke_agent_factory, L942). RoutedAgent, L415 adds decorator-dispatched message handlers, and ClosureAgent, L76 turns a bare async function into an agent. Every delivery carries a MessageContext, L9 with sender, topic, and the is_rpc flag that separates request/response from event flow.

Group Chats Are a Manager Agent Plus a Protocol

AgentChat is “just” a protocol on top of that bus. BaseGroupChat, L40 wires each participant as a ChatAgentContainer and adds one more actor: the manager (_init, L191). Wiring is all subscriptions — each participant listens on its own topic and the shared group topic, while the manager also subscribes to the output topic so streamed events reach your console.

The turn cycle is three messages. GroupChatStart, L38 reaches the manager’s handle_start; the manager decides who speaks and publishes GroupChatRequestPublish, L68; the named container runs its agent and broadcasts a GroupChatAgentResponse, L48, which lands in handle_agent_response, L135. There the manager applies the termination check (_apply_termination_condition, L195) and, if the chat lives on, _transition_to_next_speakers, L172 requests the next speaker. On the consumer side, run_stream loops on an output queue, yielding messages until a GroupChatTermination event carries the stop reason — and the caller’s cancellation token is linked to the pending receive, so a hung stream can still be killed. When the stop condition fires, the team’s stream ends via stop_when_idle and yields a TaskResult. Where LangGraph models this loop as an explicit state machine you draw (we toured that in the LangGraph internals walkthrough), AutoGen hides the edges inside a conversation protocol and a policy method.

Four Ways to Pick the Next Speaker

Every policy is the same manager base class with a different select_speaker. RoundRobinGroupChatManager, L16 just increments a cyclic index — deterministic and free. SelectorGroupChatManager, L50 asks an LLM: its select_speaker, L152 honors an optional custom selector function first, builds a roles-plus-transcript prompt, then _select_speaker, L232 retries JSON votes and falls back to mention counts (_mentioned_agents, L310).

The other two policies are conversational. The Swarm manager (SwarmGroupChatManager, L15) scans the thread backwards for the latest HandoffMessage and follows it — handoffs themselves are tool calls generated from the declarative Handoff, L12 spec via handoff_tool. And MagenticOneOrchestrator, L58 — the Magentic-One pattern — maintains a task ledger plus a JSON progress ledger: _orchestrate_step, L300 detects stalls, re-plans or redirects, and eventually _prepare_final_answer, L478 asks a designated agent to produce the answer.

Inside AssistantAgent’s Tool Loop

AssistantAgent, L90 is where the rubber meets the model. Before each call it refreshes context — including _update_model_context_with_memory, L1028, which invokes the pluggable Memory, L60 protocol so a vector-store-backed store (say, Qdrant behind your own corpus) can inject retrieved facts. If your retrieval needs outgrow agent-adjacent memory and become the product itself, that’s a data framework’s job — see our LlamaIndex source tour.

Then create or create_stream runs, and _process_model_result, L1118 loops up to max_tool_iterations: yield a ToolCallRequestEvent, execute every FunctionCall concurrently through BaseTool, L96 or a Workbench, L78 (the MCP-style tool service), emit results, and either reflect on tool use with a final LLM call (_reflect_on_tool_use_flow, L1409) or summarize. The loop is bounded, which is precisely the recovery knob a bare while-loop lacks. Streaming survives all of it: with model_client_stream=True, token chunks arrive as ModelClientStreamingChunkEvent, L529 in the same event stream your UI consumes, and tool execution results stream through an internal queue so progress is never buffered until the end.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps it to two packages: Python 3.10+ and pip install -U "autogen-agentchat" "autogen-ext[openai]" (Installation, L38). AgentChat is the high-level API; autogen-ext carries the provider clients (OpenAI, Azure, Anthropic, Ollama) plus extras like caching. Export OPENAI_API_KEY and the Hello World is eight lines (Quickstart, L53):

import asyncio
from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient

async def main() -> None:
    model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model="gpt-4.1")
    agent = AssistantAgent("assistant", model_client=model_client)
    print(await agent.run(task="Say 'Hello World!'"))
    await model_client.close()

asyncio.run(main())

Swap the agent for a RoundRobinGroupChat([agent1, agent2], termination_condition=MaxMessageTermination(10)) and you have a team; .run() returns a TaskResult with every message and the stop reason. For a no-code UI there’s AutoGen Studio (pip install -U autogenstudio).

Honest Limits

The same conversation-centric design sets the ceilings. First, every turn is a full LLM round-trip per agent, and long threads make every subsequent call bigger — group chats with LLM-based selection pay an extra selection call on top. The mitigations are explicit: token- and message-aware stops like TokenUsageTermination, L235, sentinel phrases via TextMentionTermination, L111, ExternalTermination, L404 for human-in-the-loop stops, and bounded model context via ChatCompletionContext, L10. Nothing structural stops a team from politely agreeing with itself, though — if you want hard guarantees about who runs when, a drawn graph gives you edges a conversation cannot.

Second, the runtime you get by default is single-process asyncio; scaling past one box means the gRPC worker runtime from autogen-ext, which is real distributed-systems work (message ordering, host availability) that AutoGen doesn’t hide from you. Third, v0.4 is a deliberate break: the README points v0.2 users at a migration guide (Releases, L41), and code from the old pyautogen API does not carry over. None of these are disqualifiers — they’re the cost of a framework that puts the orchestration seam in the open instead of burying it in an agent loop.

entry.title: CrewAI Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Role-Based Multi-Agent Framework

link.title: CrewAI Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Role-Based Multi-Agent Framework

entry.content:
Ask a plain chat loop to “research the market, then analyze it, then write the report” and it will happily blur all three jobs into one context window. Nothing in a bare while True: ask the model loop knows who does what. There are no roles, so no specialist pressure on the prompt. There is no accountability, so a bad sub-answer silently poisons every step after it. And there is no task order, so the model decides on its own whether analysis should wait for research — usually by cramming everything into a single response. Multi-agent frameworks exist because those three absences hurt in proportion to how much real work you route through an LLM.

CrewAI’s answer is a set of deliberately small primitives. An Agent is declared with a role, a goal and a backstory. A Task carries a description, an expected output and an agent assignment. A Crew composes them under a process mode — sequential, or hierarchical with a manager agent handing out work. Around that sits a second paradigm, Flows, where decorated methods form an event-driven state graph. The metaphor is sticky; what we wanted to know is what the code actually does with it.

This tour walks the current main branch of crewAIInc/crewAI (the framework now lives under lib/crewai/src/crewai/ in a uv workspace) and follows one kickoff from end to end. Three questions organize the dive: how a crew actually executes tasks, where the agent loop really lives (the answer surprised us — it is itself a Flow), and how hierarchical mode delegates through a manager LLM without hard-coding any routing logic.

CrewAI overview: one kickoff fans tasks through the process mode into per-task execution, the executor loop, the LLM layer, tool usage and delegation — with Flows and Memory wired around the core.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Crew.kickoff(), L997 is the single entry point: it validates the crew, merges user inputs, and dispatches by process mode.
  • Process, L4 ships exactly two modes — sequential at L9 and hierarchical at L10; a consensual mode survives only as a TODO comment.
  • Crew._execute_tasks(), L1577 is the real task queue: synchronous tasks run in order while async ones park in futures that are drained before the next sync task blocks on them.
  • Task._execute_core(), L844 resolves the assigned agent, emits a TaskStartedEvent, then calls the agent — this is where declarative task meets runtime.
  • Agent.execute_task(), L978 assembles the final prompt from the role, goal and backstory fields declared on BaseAgent, L255, folding in retrieved knowledge first.
  • AgentExecutor, L203 is the tool-calling loop — and it is literally a Flow[AgentExecutorState], so CrewAI runs its own agent loop on its own orchestration engine.
  • BaseLLM.call(), L541 defines the one abstract chat contract; the concrete LLM, L276 class routes every provider through LiteLLM.
  • DelegateWorkTool, L16 is how the hierarchical manager hands work sideways, while ToolUsage, L84 executes ordinary tool requests with limits and caching.

CrewAI internals: the detail graph expands each stage into grep-verified functions, from the kickoff dispatch and the task loop down to prompt assembly, the executor loop, delegation and the memory subsystem.

From Kickoff to Task Queue

kickoff() at crew.py, L997 does configuration validation first — hierarchical crews must provide a manager_llm or manager_agent (L734) — then hands off to a process runner. Sequential mode is a one-liner: _run_sequential_process(), L1524 just calls _execute_tasks(self.tasks).

The loop itself is where CrewAI earns the word “crew”. _execute_tasks() at L1577 iterates the task list, and for each task a helper (prepare_task_execution(), L118) resolves which agent takes it — normally the task’s own agent, but the crew’s manager under hierarchical mode (L499). Tasks marked async_execution are kicked off as futures (L1620); the next synchronous task first drains all pending futures (L1627) so its context is complete. That context comes from _get_context(), L1887, which concatenates prior TaskOutput, L15 objects into a string the next prompt can quote. This is the entire data flow between tasks: no shared blackboard, just ordered outputs threading forward.

The loop also absorbs the edge cases you would otherwise hand-roll. ConditionalTask instances are checked against prior outputs and skipped when their condition fails (_handle_conditional_task(), L1648), replayable crews resume from the first task that has no stored output (_get_execution_start_index(), L1569), and kickoff_for_each() at L1101 fans one crew definition across a list of inputs — a built-in map over batch jobs.

Inside the Agent Loop

Each task bottoms out in Task._execute_core(), L844: it publishes TaskStartedEvent on the global event bus (CrewAIEventsBus, L95, instantiated once at L952), then calls Agent.execute_task(), L978.

Prompt construction happens in three stages. _prepare_task_execution(), L699 renders the role/goal/backstory template with the task description; _finalize_task_prompt(), L727 appends tool descriptions, expected output and stop words. Knowledge retrieval sits between them: agents (and crews) query a Knowledge, L88 source and inline the matches (L1007). The finished prompt goes to the executor via _execute_without_timeout(), L1090, whose body is one agent_executor.invoke(...) call.

The executor is the surprise. AgentExecutor, L203 subclasses both BaseAgentExecutor and Flow[AgentExecutorState] (state, L165) — the think/act cycle is modeled as a state graph, closer to the explicit graph machines of LangGraph than to a hand-rolled while loop. Its tool requests flow into ToolUsage, L84, which respects per-task limits and calls BaseTool.run(), L353 to validate args before _run(). The LLM call itself is provider-neutral: BaseLLM.call(), L541 is the contract, and LLM, L276 imports LiteLLM lazily (L137) so any provider/model string works.

Memory slots into the same seam. When a crew opts in, a scoped Memory, L76 instance backs its tasks: recall(), L686 surfaces similar prior records while the prompt is being finalized, and remember(), L435 encodes finished outputs for future runs. Backends stay pluggable through resolve_memory_storage(), L48, so the vector store is a deployment decision rather than a framework commitment. Everything the loop touches is observable, too — the same event bus that announced the task also carries LLM, tool and memory events for listeners and tracing.

How Hierarchical Delegation Actually Works

Flip the crew to Process.hierarchical and _run_hierarchical_process(), L1528 first builds the manager. _create_manager_agent(), L1533 constructs an Agent from manager_llm whose role, goal and backstory come straight from the prompt templates (I18N.retrieve(), L100) — and whose tools are AgentTools(agents=self.agents).tools(), L22. That is the whole trick: the manager is not routing code, it is a regular role-playing agent whose toolbox happens to be its crewmates.

Two tools make up that toolbox. DelegateWorkTool, L16 takes a task, context and coworker role; its _run(), L22 calls BaseAgentTools._execute(), L46, which matches the role case-insensitively, builds a one-off Task (L112) and re-enters the same execute_task(), L120 path as a normal task. AskQuestionTool, L14 is the clarification variant. One guardrail is explicit: a custom manager_agent must not carry its own tools, or _create_manager_agent raises outright (L1548). For non-hierarchical crews, _add_delegation_tools(), L1839 wires a lighter version per agent, and _update_manager_tools(), L1872 keeps the manager’s set in sync per task. Accountability, in other words, is just tool-call provenance: every hand-off is visible as a delegation event.

Flows: The Second Orchestration

Crews answer “who does this work”; Flows answer “in what order, triggered by what”. The public Flow, L37 is a thin facade over the runtime engine in flow/runtime/__init__.py, L444, whose metaclass (FlowMeta, L391) scans your class for decorated methods. @start, L18 marks entries, @listen, L18 wires a method to fire when another updates typed state (FlowState, L376), and kickoff(), L2116 orders and runs the graph. Triggers compose: the README documents or_ and and_ combinators usable on @start, @listen and @router conditions (L440). Because a flow method can call crew.kickoff() internally, the two paradigms nest: deterministic control flow outside, role-based teamwork inside.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps onboarding short. CrewAI needs Python 3.10 or newer but under 3.14, and installs as a uv tool: uv tool install crewai (README, L226). Scaffold a project with crewai create crew latest-ai-development (L304) — current scaffolding is JSON-first, with agents in agents/*.jsonc and tasks plus process settings in crew.jsonc (L260); the older YAML layout survives behind --classic (L286). Each agent file is just role, goal, backstory, llm string and tools. Then crewai run executes it. If you prefer code over JSON, the README’s flow example (L457) shows the full shape: a @start method, an @listen method that builds a Crew with Process.sequential, L493 and returns analysis_crew.kickoff(inputs=...) (L496). Set an OPENAI_API_KEY-style variable for your chosen provider and the first model call works without further config.

Honest Limits

Read the source and the metaphor’s edges show. Role adherence is prompt discipline only: role, goal and backstory (L255) are interpolated text, and nothing at runtime stops an agent from wandering off-persona. Hierarchical mode is genuinely costly — the manager is a separate LLM-driven agent (L1550), so every delegation is extra tokens and latency, and delegation quality depends on the model emitting valid JSON tool arguments; the code itself carries a comment about less-powerful LLMs truncating exactly that JSON (L66). Only two process modes ship (L11). Memory (Memory, L76, with recall at L686 and remember at L435) resolves pluggable backends at runtime (L48), which adds deployment moving parts. The license is MIT, and the README delegates the full walkthrough to docs.crewai.com rather than duplicating it.

If you want a second opinion on the design space, compare this with AutoGen’s conversation-driven agents at /autogen-runtime/, the explicit graph machines behind agent loops at /langgraph-internals/, the composable Runnable abstraction at /langchain/, or the retrieval-first data layer at /llama-index/.
entry.summary: A grep-verified source tour of CrewAI's main branch: how Crew.kickoff fans out through _execute_tasks, where the AgentExecutor tool-calling loop lives, and how hierarchical mode delegates through a manager LLM.

entry.title: Haystack Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Type-Safe RAG Orchestration Engine

link.title: Haystack Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Type-Safe RAG Orchestration Engine

entry.content:
Every LLM application eventually hits the same failure: stage two was refactored, stage three still expects the old shape, and nothing tells you until 3 a.m. in production when the retriever hands the prompt builder a string instead of a list of documents. Early LangChain-style composition made this worse by passing free-form dicts between steps — we walked through that design in our LangChain source tour — and dynamic graphs only move the guesswork from composition time to execution time. The error is real, the stack trace is useless, and the fix is a hopeful print statement.

Haystack 2.x, deepset’s orchestration framework, attacks the problem from the opposite direction. Every component declares typed input and output sockets; a graph object wires sockets to sockets; and the connect() call validates every edge against Python typing rules before anything runs. Mis-wire a graph and the build itself refuses to complete, with an error naming both sides and their types. Where LangGraph internals run a dynamic state machine that reads its own state to decide the next node, and CrewAI orchestrates by role-play between personas, Haystack is the static-typed counterpoint: a directed graph whose legality is proven at construction, then executed mechanically.

This tour reads the main branch (November 2026, heading toward 3.0) to see exactly how that guarantee is implemented: how the component decorator turns run() signatures into typed sockets, how connect() rejects incompatible edges while permitting genuine cycles, how the run loop schedules components through a priority queue over a networkx multi-graph, and where agents, tools, tracing, and breakpoints slot into the same execution model.

Overview: authoring flows left to right into graph construction, then the runtime queue; agents and tools hang off the same execution path as ordinary leaf components.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The decorator is the front door. component = _Component(), L635 is a singleton: apply it to any class with a run() method and it becomes a first-class graph node.
  • Sockets are the contract. InputSocket, L39 and OutputSocket, L124 carry a declared type plus an optional default; the type is what every later check compares.
  • Registration is validation. add_component, L397 checks the instance and inserts it as a named node — a component with no valid run() never gets in.
  • Wiring is type-checked. connect, L586 enumerates socket candidates on both sides and consults _types_are_compatible, L295 for each pair.
  • The graph is a real graph library object. networkx.MultiDiGraph(), L115 stores nodes and edges, with edge keys built from socket names.
  • Cycles are first-class. _topological_sort, L1506 takes a fast path for DAGs and otherwise condenses strongly connected components so looping graphs stay deterministic.
  • Scheduling is a priority queue, not recursion. run, L200 drains a FIFOPriorityQueue, L87 ranked by ComponentPriority, L79.
  • Every execution is instrumented. _run_component, L127 opens a tracing span, counts visits, and wraps failures with component context; spans flow through ProxyTracer, L106.
  • Agents and tools are components too. Agent.run, L882 and Tool.invoke, L269 plug into the same socket contract as a plain generator.

Detail: the component model feeds connect-time validation, which feeds the execution engine; agents, tools, super components, and tracing wrap the same core.

Components: Types Declared, Not Assumed

The contract starts at instantiation, not at run time. When you construct a decorated class, ComponentMeta.__call__ (L285) parses run(): each parameter becomes an InputSocket, each annotated return value an OutputSocket. If run() has an unsubstantiated signature, construction fails on the spot — a broken component cannot even be created, let alone wired. For dynamic cases, set_input_type (L414) re-declares a single socket after the fact, which is how varargs-style components widen their inputs legitimately.

The metaclass is strict in both directions: _compare_run_methods_signatures (L352) rejects a class whose synchronous run() and run_async() disagree, so the async mirror of a component cannot silently drift from its sync twin — one class serves both schedulers, and the parse of its signature (L232) happens exactly once, at instantiation.

This is the quiet difference from framework ecosystems where components exchange untyped bags of data. In Haystack the question “what does this component accept?” has a machine-readable answer at all times, and the graph owner can therefore validate structure — add_component, L397 — and semantics — the wiring — mechanically. PydanticAI reaches a similar safety goal for agents with pydantic-validated tool signatures; Haystack applies the same discipline to the whole graph.

connect(): The Build-Time Gatekeeper

connect("retriever", "ranker") looks innocent, but the implementation is a small type engine. First parse_connect_string (L72) splits component.socket notation. Then connect (L586) gathers sender and receiver socket candidates and runs the compatibility check on each pair; a match may also yield a conversion strategy, so some near-misses are bridged automatically instead of rejected. Zero matches produces the error every Haystack user has memorized: “their declared input and output types do not match” — naming both sides and both types (L704).

Two refinements make it practical. When several senders target one receiver, _make_socket_auto_variadic (L1166) converts the receiver to variadic so it collects a list — that is how fan-in works without user ceremony. And when more than one socket pair could match, connect refuses to guess and tells you to name the sockets explicitly. Every ambiguity is resolved at build time or not at all.

The Run Loop: A Priority Queue Over a MultiDiGraph

Execution begins with run() (L200) validating top-level inputs against the graph’s sockets (validate_input, L1126), then computing order. The topological sort is worth reading: DAGs get a lexicographic sort for determinism, while cyclic graphs go through networkx.condensation (L1523) so every component inside a cycle shares a priority and can iterate until its inputs say stop.

From there the loop is mechanical: _calculate_priority (L1412) ranks entries READY through BLOCKED into the FIFO queue, _get_next_runnable_component (L1453) pops the next candidate, and _run_component (L127) does one unit of work — breakpoint check, tracing span, instance.run(**inputs), then verification that the result is a mapping with only declared keys and a bumped visit count. _write_component_outputs (L1653) routes each output to receiver sockets, applying conversion strategies, which re-enables downstream components. Failures are re-raised wrapped with component name and class, so a stack trace tells you which node died. Stalls are diagnosed rather than suffered silently: a dedicated validator inspects a stuck queue (L1755), a sibling helper names exactly which components block progress (L1572), and _tiebreak_waiting_components (L1529) breaks remaining ties deterministically. The async engine reuses the same ideas rather than reimplementing them: _run_component_async (L543) mirrors the sync executor, _wait_for_tasks (L615) gathers concurrent branches, and in-flight work is cancelled cleanly when one branch fails (L647). Lifecycle hooks complete the model — warm_up (L1040) loads model weights once before the first request, close (L1070) releases them, and to_dict/from_dict (L152) round-trip the assembled graph for storage. The public surface stays symmetric: run_async (L1099) awaits one result, run_async_generator (L808) yields partial results as branches finish, and stream (L1212) wraps token-level streaming into the same contract.

Agents and Tools Inside the Same Graph

The elegant part is that agentic behavior does not fork the execution model. Agent (L266) is an ordinary component whose run (L882) “processes messages and executes tools until an exit condition is met.” Internally, _run_step (L1070) performs one chat-generator call plus every tool call the model requested, and _check_exit_conditions (L1208) decides whether to continue; the result reports step_count, token_usage, tool_call_counts, and an exit_reason you can route on. Unlike CrewAI’s persona crews, this is one reusable component with hooks, not a cast of characters.

Tools follow the same philosophy. Tool.invoke (L269) validates arguments against the tool’s schema before calling the wrapped function, and invoke_async (L293) gives async callers the same check; ComponentTool (L35) promotes any component into a tool; AgentTool (L51) promotes an entire agent into one — agents composing agents. There is even a wrapper that exposes a whole graph as a single tool (L21). Composition scales the other way too: SuperComponent (L412) wraps an inner graph behind a normal component interface with explicit input/output mappings, and the runner flattens those sub-graphs before execution (L1786). Because agents are components, they inherit the housekeeping too: warm_up (L639) primes the generator and tools, and clone (L671) forks an agent mid-flight for per-request customization. Observability threads through everything: enable_tracing (L165) swaps the null tracer for a real one, and breakpoints can halt a run and persist a snapshot (L141).

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps onboarding honest and short: pip install haystack-ai (L32), or pip install --pre haystack-ai (L37) for nightly builds. From there the README deliberately hands you to the Get Started Guide and tutorials rather than inlining a long example — the repo assumes you will learn by building. The build itself is always the same four moves, each of which we have already seen in the source: instantiate a generator such as OpenAIChatGenerator (L62, whose key comes from the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable at L130), register it and a retriever with add_component, wire them with connect, and call run() with your question. Call warm_up() first and the models load once, outside the request path — the engine exposes the hook on the whole graph, and every component implements the same method. Because generators exist for OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Hugging Face, and local models, swapping vendors is a one-line change to the component — the graph and its type checks do not move (README L67-68).

Honest Limits

The static bet has costs. Cycles, branches, and agent loops are supported, but they must be expressed as graph structure — variadic receivers, visit counts, exit conditions — whereas a dynamic state machine lets you write arbitrary control flow imperatively. If your problem is genuinely procedural rather than a flow of typed stages, Haystack’s rigidity buys you less. The 2.x to 3.0 transition is documented in MIGRATION.md (L3) and includes a serialization format break (L9) plus the move of many components into separate integration packages (L35) — audit your integrations before upgrading. Graph YAML round-trips through dumps/loads (L293) with a dedicated security module guarding deserialization, but treat shared graph files as untrusted input nonetheless. Finally, the README’s feature sections read more like marketing than documentation, and anonymous telemetry fires on component initialization (L89) — both are opt-out-able but worth knowing before you standardize on the framework.
entry.summary: A source tour of deepset's Haystack: typed components, build-time graph validation in connect(), and an explicit run loop that keeps LLM apps from crashing in production.

entry.title: LangChain Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Framework Behind Millions of LLM Apps

link.title: LangChain Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Framework Behind Millions of LLM Apps

entry.content:
Every LLM application eventually turns into the same pile of glue. You concatenate prompts, wrap a provider SDK call in retry logic, parse replies with string hacks, feed tool results back into the conversation, and stitch retrieved documents from a vector store such as Qdrant into the context. Then a provider ships a new API, or you add a second model vendor, and the glue multiplies: streaming shapes differ, function-calling formats differ, error taxonomies differ. The interesting part of your application drowns in plumbing.

LangChain’s bet is that this plumbing deserves its own layer, and millions of LLM apps have agreed. The framework reduces the chaos to a short list of abstractions: standardized messages, a BaseChatModel contract, composable Runnables, schema-carrying tools, and, since the 1.0 restructuring, a single factory function named create_agent. Read the source and the mystique evaporates: an “agent” is a compiled LangGraph state machine with a model node, a tools node, and a conditional edge that loops until the model stops requesting tools. That is genuinely all it is — and it turns out to be enough.

This tour reads the master branch of langchain-ai/langchain as it exists after the v1.0 reorganization: framework primitives live in libs/core/langchain_core, the v1 langchain package in libs/langchain_v1, and vendor integrations under libs/partners. Two diagrams anchor the walk — an overview of the main flow and a detail map of the internals — and every symbol cited below was verified in the tree, with line numbers you can click through to GitHub.

Figure 1 — LangChain's main flow: messages enter a chat model, responses come back as messages, and the agent loop wires models and tools into a LangGraph state machine wrapped by middleware.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Input is normalized into messages first: HumanMessage, L9 extends BaseMessage, L93, so every component speaks one data format.
  • BaseChatModel, L325 is the single model contract: invoke (L516) delegates to generate (L1635), which finally calls the abstract _generate (L2252) that providers implement.
  • Replies are messages too: AIMessage, L160 carries content plus tool_calls, the field that drives the entire agent loop.
  • Runnable, L197 gives models, parsers, tools and lambdas one invoke/batch/stream surface; the | operator composes them into a RunnableSequence, L3094.
  • RunnableSequence.invoke, L3449 is the heart of composition: a plain for-loop over steps, opening a child callback run per step and piping each output forward.
  • BaseTool, L433 makes tools Runnables with a schema; run (L1009) validates arguments against args_schema before dispatching to _run (L909).
  • create_agent, L892 builds the loop: a StateGraph, L1239 gets a model node (L1611) and a tools node (L1615), then graph.compile() (L1909) returns the agent.
  • AgentMiddleware, L385 injects before_model (L455), after_model (L479) and wrap_model_call (L503) hooks around the loop without any subclassing.

Figure 2 — The internals: message hierarchy, the generate path down to provider hooks, runnable composition and resilience wrappers, tool validation, and the exact graph wiring inside create_agent.

One Contract for Every Provider

Open libs/core/langchain_core/language_models/chat_models.py and you find the layer that made LangChain famous: BaseChatModel, L325 owns everything except the HTTP call. The public entry point invoke (L516) normalizes input and opens a callback run; generate (L1635) adds batching, cache lookups and usage accounting; only at the bottom does the abstract _generate (L2252) appear — the one method a provider package like langchain-openai must write. Streaming follows the same split: the default stream, L770 implementation uses the provider’s _stream when available and otherwise falls back to chunked generation, so every model “just streams” from the caller’s perspective. Throttling lives in the base class too: a rate_limiter field (L375) is acquired with blocking=True inside generate (L1978) and the streaming paths (L829) before any request leaves the process, which is why swapping providers does not mean rewriting your backoff logic.

Construction is string-driven and lazy. init_chat_model, L197 parses identifiers like openai:gpt-5.5 via _parse_model (L623), infers the provider from name prefixes when you omit it (L547), and imports the integration package on demand. Swapping vendors is a string edit, which is the entire point of the abstraction.

Runnables: Why the Pipe Operator Works

Anything with Runnable, L197 in its ancestry exposes the same surface, so prompt | model | parser is one object you can invoke, stream, batch or save. RunnableSequence.invoke, L3449 iterates self.steps, starting a child callback run per step and feeding each output to the next input. Plain functions join chains through RunnableLambda, L4722, and fan-out maps are handled by RunnableParallel (L3883).

Resilience is composition too. .with_retry() (L2153) wraps any step in RunnableRetry, L50 with exponential backoff, and .with_fallbacks() (L2243) produces a RunnableWithFallbacks, L37 that tries alternates on failure. Parsers close the loop: StrOutputParser, L8 extends BaseOutputParser, L140, itself a Runnable, and JsonOutputParser (L32 in json.py) feeds structured output to your code. Retrieval fits the same shape — a similarity search against FAISS or another index is just another step in the sequence.

Batching shows the engine room. RunnableSequence.batch, L3525 runs step i across all surviving inputs before moving to step i + 1 — true stepwise batching, not a loop of independent chains. Each per-step child run is named seq:step:N (L3587), and a failure map (L3569) tracks inputs that already errored so downstream steps skip them when return_exceptions is set.

The Agent Is a Two-Node Graph

create_agent, L892 is where the “agent” keyword dissolves. Its docstring says it plainly: it “creates an agent graph that calls tools in a loop until a stopping condition is met” (L912). A string model is resolved through init_chat_model (L1048); the factory then builds a StateGraph, L1239 over an AgentState whose core field is the message list, binds tools in _get_bound_model (L1350), and registers exactly two nodes: model_node (L1520, added at L1611) and the tools node (L1615), skipped entirely when you pass no tools. A conditional edge inspects the last AIMessage: if it carries tool_calls, the graph emits Send(‘tools’, …), L2032 — one per call — otherwise the loop ends and graph.compile() (L1909) hands back a runnable graph. Structured output rides the same loop: a response_format argument accepts a Pydantic schema or a ToolStrategy/ProviderStrategy (per the factory docstring, L954), and matching structured tool calls are intercepted before they reach the tools node.

Two details deserve attention. First, the tools node is not reimplemented: LangChain re-exports ToolNode from langgraph.prebuilt through a one-line shim, L4, so execution semantics live in the LangGraph runtime. Second, because the agent is a graph, persistence is native — pass a checkpointer and conversation state survives invocations, a pattern you can back with Postgres for durable, multi-session agents. What reads as “a loop” is literally a small graph with explicit hops: the START edge lands at the entry node (L1743) and after-model middleware edges are wired one hop past the model node (L1857).

Middleware Instead of Subclasses

Version 1 replaced the old executor-style customization with an interceptor list. AgentMiddleware, L385 declares before_model, L455 and after_model, L479, which run around every model call and may rewrite state, plus wrap_model_call, L503, an onion-style wrapper around the request itself, and before_agent/after_agent (L431/L650) bracketing the whole run. The request a wrapper sees is a typed ModelRequest (L88) — messages, model handle and runtime context — so a hook can edit what the model is about to receive without touching the graph. The factory wires each hook into the graph as real nodes and edges — after-model hooks literally become graph hops (L1857).

A standard library of middleware ships alongside: SummarizationMiddleware, L262 compresses history when it outgrows a trigger, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware, L397 pauses for approve/edit/reject decisions on risky tools, and ModelFallbackMiddleware (L342) plus ModelRetryMiddleware (L33) add provider-level resilience. Because middleware declares its own state fields, features compose without inheritance — the same philosophy that makes external caches such as Redis easy to bolt onto a running agent.

From Install to Your First Model

The README quickstart is deliberately short. Install with uv add langchain, then:

from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model

model = init_chat_model("openai:gpt-5.5")
result = model.invoke("Hello, world!")

On first call, init_chat_model routes to _init_chat_model_helper (L536): the string is split by _parse_model (L623), the provider is matched against the built-in registry (L56) or inferred from the model-name prefix, and _get_chat_model_creator (L153) uses importlib to import the integration package — langchain-openai for the openai key. If that package is missing you get an ImportError naming the exact pip install target (L147), which is the framework’s intended discovery mechanism. Passing a bare model name like claude-... works too via prefix heuristics. To go from chat to agent, hand the same string to create_agent with a tools list; the factory resolves it identically and returns a compiled graph you can invoke, stream or checkpoint.

Honest Limits

  • Indirection has a price. One invoke crosses invoke → generate → _generate → the provider client, and inside an agent those layers sit under a LangGraph execution as well. Stack traces span several frames before you reach your bug.
  • Version churn is real. The 1.0 restructuring split the monorepo: legacy code ships as langchain_classic under libs/langchain, the v1 package lives in libs/langchain_v1, and imports moved with them. Pre-2025 tutorials routinely reference paths that no longer resolve.
  • Quirks are encapsulated, not eliminated. The _generate hook still carries provider-specific kwargs, rate limits and streaming caveats; the standard interface hides differences but does not remove the need to read provider documentation.
  • Overhead for trivial apps. A single one-shot LLM call wrapped in callback managers and runnable metadata buys little; the abstractions pay off only once you compose steps, retry, stream or loop.
  • Docs caveats. The repository README is a landing page: a three-line quickstart and links. Integration-package install guidance first appears inside ImportError messages, and the real documentation lives off-repo at docs.langchain.com.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of LangChain's master branch: chat models, runnables, tools, the create_agent loop and middleware, with two verified architecture diagrams.

entry.title: LangGraph Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the State Machine Running Modern AI Agents

link.title: LangGraph Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the State Machine Running Modern AI Agents

entry.content:
Almost every demo agent works, and almost every production agent eventually does not. The model calls the same tool in a loop until the context window fills, a crash at step fourteen throws away the previous thirteen, and there is nowhere to insert a human approval exactly where money leaves the building. None of that is a model problem. It is a control-flow problem, and control flow is precisely the layer that most agent frameworks leave implicit.

LangGraph, the orchestration engine underneath LangChain’s agent runtime, makes that layer explicit. Its primitives map one-to-one onto the failure modes: state is a set of typed channels with reducer functions, work is graph nodes executed in Pregel-style supersteps, every step is persisted to a pluggable checkpointer, and any node can raise an interrupt that pauses the graph until a human answers. In our LangChain source tour we watched create_agent compile down to a StateGraph — this post goes one level lower, into the machine that executes it.

We cloned the langchain-ai/langgraph monorepo at main and traced the path a run actually takes: the builder you write, the compile step that turns it into a Pregel instance, the loop that plans and executes tasks against channels, and the checkpoint and interrupt machinery that makes the whole thing resumable. The recurring discovery is that every headline “agent” feature is just a graph pattern with a name. The two diagrams below were generated from that walkthrough.

Figure 1 — The full flight path: a StateGraph builder compiles into the Pregel engine, whose superstep loop plans tasks, runs them against channels, snapshots checkpoints, and pauses on interrupts.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The builder is a schema interpreter. StateGraph, L131 reads your TypedDict state definition and turns each key into a channel; add_node, L376 and add_conditional_edges, L982 register functions and routers rather than “steps” — nothing runs yet.
  • Compile does not build a new runtime — it becomes one. StateGraph.compile, L1177 returns a CompiledStateGraph, L1404, which subclasses Pregel directly. Your graph and its engine are one object.
  • The engine is a loop, not a scheduler. Pregel, L456 exposes the Runnable interface (stream, L2728, astream, L3179), but each run is just repeated iterations of PregelLoop, L172.
  • One tick, one superstep. PregelLoop.tick, L652 takes the channel writes from the previous step, plans which nodes fire next, and submits them to PregelRunner.tick, L173, which runs them concurrently.
  • State updates go through apply_writes, L234, which pushes node outputs into channels and bumps per-channel versions — the version map is what decides what runs in the next superstep.
  • Channels are the reducers. LastValue, L20 keeps one write per step, Topic, L23 appends everything, and add_messages, L64 merges message lists by ID. Parallel tool calls cannot clobber each other because conflict resolution is a channel policy, not an accident.
  • Checkpoints ride the loop. Every superstep the loop calls the saver contract at BaseCheckpointSaver, L199 (InMemorySaver, L34 is the reference backend).
  • Interrupts are exceptions with a mailbox. interrupt, L913 raises GraphInterrupt, L104; the caller resumes with Command, L843. Human-in-the-loop is a raised exception plus a checkpoint, nothing more.
  • The famous react agent is a two-node graph. create_react_agent, L278 wires “agent” and “tools” nodes (add_node calls, L867) plus one conditional edge and compiles it — the same primitives you would use by hand.

Figure 2 — The detail view: compile-time wiring on the left, the per-run superstep machinery in the middle, and the channel, checkpoint, and interrupt contracts on the right.

State Is a Set of Channels, Not a Variable

The core design decision is that agent state is never a mutable object passed around. Each key of your state schema becomes a channel instance, and each channel owns its own merge policy. The default is LastValue, L20: if two concurrent nodes write different values in the same superstep, update refuses rather than silently picking one. When you want accumulation, you use Topic, L23, which keeps every write, or BinaryOperatorAggregate, L66, which folds concurrent writes through any binary operator you supply. EphemeralValue, L15 holds a value for exactly one superstep — compile uses it for the START channel that delivers your initial input (state.py, L1354).

Messages get special treatment because they are the universal agent state: add_messages, L64 deduplicates by message ID, replaces in place when a full message with the same ID arrives, and appends otherwise. That single function is why streaming partial updates and parallel tool messages coexist without corruption.

The Superstep Loop: How Nodes Actually Run

compile walks your builder spec and calls attach_node, L1444 for each node, then attach_edge and attach_branch for the wiring — the compiled object is a Pregel (main.py, L456), not a wrapper around one. When you invoke it, PregelLoop.tick, L652 runs the classic Pregel algorithm from Google’s systems research (the README credits it explicitly):

  1. prepare_single_task, L524 reads the current values of the channels a node subscribes to and binds them into an executable task. If a router returned Send, L748 objects, the planner creates one task per item — that is the whole map-reduce API.
  2. PregelRunner.tick, L173 executes the task functions concurrently and collects their channel writes as they complete.
  3. apply_writes, L234 applies the writes, updates channel versions, and marks which channels changed.
  4. The next tick re-plans from the version map. When nothing new is pending, the run ends.

Two safeguards are visible in the same files. The stop condition at PregelLoop, L1917 enforces recursion_limit, so a model that keeps requesting tools hits a hard ceiling instead of an infinite bill. And should_interrupt, L157 checks, per task, whether interrupt_before or interrupt_after applies — the pause points are just nodes on a version-aware list.

Checkpoints: Durable Execution Is Just put() and get_tuple()

The loop’s checkpoint habit is the reason crash recovery works. At each step boundary, _put_checkpoint, L1267 serializes the channel state plus pending writes and hands it to a saver. The saver contract is tiny: BaseCheckpointSaver, L199 requires put (L301) to store a checkpoint keyed by thread_id, get_tuple (L262) to load the latest one for a thread, and put_writes to record outputs of tasks that finished out of band.

Because the contract is small, durability is a backend choice. InMemorySaver, L34 is a dict-backed reference implementation for tests; the same monorepo ships Postgres and SQLite savers, and a Redis cache backend lives alongside them. Reusing a thread_id across invocations is what turns a stateless graph into a conversation — compile’s own docstring (state.py, L1208) makes that the documented memory mechanism. We compared the storage side of this problem in our PostgreSQL source tour and the caching side in the Redis tour; LangGraph simply picks a narrow interface so those backends can be swapped in without touching graph code.

Interrupts: Human-in-the-Loop Is an Exception, Not a Flag

The interrupt design is the most instructive part of the codebase. Calling interrupt, L913 inside a node raises GraphInterrupt, L104, which bubbles up through the runner and out of the superstep like any exception. The payload travels with it; the state is already safe because a checkpoint exists. The graph stops.

Resuming is where it gets clever: you invoke the graph again with Command(resume=...), and map_command, L56 converts that resume value into channel writes. The node that raised the interrupt re-executes from its start, the interrupt() call now returns the human’s answer instead of raising, and execution continues. The docstring is explicit that this requires a checkpointer (types.py, L934) — human-in-the-loop is durability applied to a pause, not a separate subsystem. The same Command type doubles as a routing primitive, so a node can update state and jump elsewhere in one return value.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps onboarding to one line: pip install -U langgraph (README.md, L27). From there, everything in this article is reachable with four calls, all verified in the source:

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from typing_extensions import TypedDict

class State(TypedDict):
    text: str

def shout(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"text": state["text"].upper()}

graph = StateGraph(State)
graph.add_node("shout", shout)
graph.add_edge(START, "shout")
graph.add_edge("shout", END)
app = graph.compile()
print(app.invoke({"text": "hello"}))

START and END are interned sentinel strings (constants.py, L28-L30) that compile special-cases. When you would rather skip the plumbing, create_react_agent assembles the model-plus-tools pattern for you: it builds a StateGraph, adds the two nodes and the should_continue, L831 router that inspects tool_calls, and returns workflow.compile(...) (chat_agent_executor.py, L995). That is the exact seam we saw from the other side in the LangChain walkthrough; teams that prefer a different abstraction style can compare it with our LlamaIndex source tour.

Honest Limits

The price of explicit control flow is verbosity: a three-node graph is more ceremony than a plain chain call, and for straight-line LLM requests LangGraph is the wrong tool. The monorepo also moves fast in ways that hurt importers — prebuilt agents now live in a separate libs/prebuilt package, checkpoint savers in libs/checkpoint, and several internals were relocated under langgraph._internal; importing them from the old paths emits deprecation warnings (constants.py, L34). Pin your version and read the changelog before upgrading.

Checkpointing has caveats too. Checkpoints are serialized through the msgpack-based serde layer, and strict mode builds an allowlist from your state schemas (state.py, L1234) — exotic custom objects in state will surface as serialization errors, not silent failures. And InMemorySaver is exactly what its name says: process-local memory for tests, not production persistence. Finally, resume semantics re-run a node from its beginning (the interrupt docstring states this directly), so any code before an interrupt() call must be idempotent — that is a real design constraint, not an implementation detail.
entry.summary: A grep-verified tour of the LangGraph source: how StateGraph compiles into a Pregel engine, how channel reducers merge agent state, and how checkpoints and interrupts make agents durable and resumable.

entry.title: LlamaIndex Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the RAG Engine Powering Data-Aware LLM Apps

link.title: LlamaIndex Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the RAG Engine Powering Data-Aware LLM Apps

entry.content:
Ask an LLM about your internal wiki, your support tickets, or last quarter’s contracts and it will answer fluently — and wrong, because it has never seen any of them. The obvious fix is to dump your documents into a vector store and paste the nearest chunks into the prompt. That naive recipe is exactly why so many RAG demos die in production: chunks are cut blind, every edit re-embeds the whole corpus, duplicates pile up, and nobody notices the prompt silently overflowing the model’s context window until answers degrade.

LlamaIndex is the engineering answer to that mess. Instead of one “throw text at the database” call, it makes the whole path explicit — ingest → parse → embed → index → retrieve → synthesize — and defines an interface at every arrow. Readers produce documents, a splitter turns them into nodes with token budgets, an embedder turns nodes into vectors, any vector store holds them, retrievers query them, and a response synthesizer turns the hits back into prose. Each stage can be swapped (OpenAI for Ollama, a built-in store for Qdrant) without touching the others.

Reading the source makes the design click in a way no tutorial does: the QueryEngine you call in the quickstart is nothing but a retriever wired to a response synthesizer, with a callback manager tracing every stage transition; agents are a separate event-driven loop layered on top that treats query engines as tools. This tour walks the actual code on the main branch, and the two diagrams map the full topology, from the first Document to the final synthesized answer.

Overview: the left-to-right flow from Document to answer. The top row is ingestion, the middle the storage contract and index, the bottom retrieval and synthesis, and the right column the runtime layer.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Readers normalize the world into documents. SimpleDirectoryReader, L208 walks a folder and emits Document objects (Document, L1097), the backward-compatible subclass of TextNode, L765.
  • Chunking is sentence-aware and token-budgeted. SentenceSplitter, L34 merges sentence splits until they fill a chunk (split_text, L176); the default is 1024 tokens (DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE, L10).
  • One flow chains all transformations. The ingestion runner applies each transformation in order (ConfiguredTransformation, L347) while IngestionCache, L17 lets re-runs skip documents whose content hash is unchanged.
  • Embeddings are an interface, not a vendor. BaseEmbedding, L72 is itself a transform component: get_text_embedding, L385 for one text, get_text_embedding_batch, L486 for bulk, and an async twin at L439.
  • The store contract is one query object. VectorStoreQuery, L240 carries the embedding, similarity_top_k, mode and filters; SimpleVectorStore, L64 is the in-memory reference that provider stores swap in for (its query, L244).
  • The index is surprisingly thin. VectorStoreIndex, L36 only batch-embeds missing vectors and delegates (_add_nodes_to_index, L219, build_index_from_nodes, L286).
  • Retrievers wrap stores, not indices. VectorIndexRetriever, L24 overrides _retrieve, L104 of BaseRetriever, L34, whose public retrieve, L192 handles callbacks and recursion around it.
  • A query engine is just glue. RetrieverQueryEngine, L25 composes via from_args, L63: retrieve, postprocess, then synthesize (_query, L203).
  • Everything is traced and globally wired. CallbackManager, L28 fans events out to handlers (on_event_start, L88), and the Settings singleton, L19 supplies default LLM and embed models.

The detail diagram drops into each stage, following the two separate axes the code actually has: the write path (documents to stored vectors) and the read path (query string to synthesized answer).

Detail view: 33 components across ingestion, embedding, storage, index construction, retrieval, synthesis and the runtime that wires them together. Every box links to the exact source file in the repository.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s quickstart maps one-to-one onto the diagram. Two install styles exist: the batteries-included llama-index starter, or core plus hand-picked provider packages (pip install llama-index-core, then pip install llama-index-llms-openai and friends). With an OPENAI_API_KEY in the environment, the canonical three lines are SimpleDirectoryReader("YOUR_DATA_DIRECTORY").load_data() followed by VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents) — and [from_documents, L89](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/indices/base.py#L89) is literally the write path from the detail diagram compressed into one call. Querying is index.as_query_engine().query("..."), and [as_query_engine, L491](https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/main/llama-index-core/llama_index/core/indices/base.py#L491) just calls the same factory the diagram shows. Everything defaults to OpenAI through the global Settings object; for fully local stacks the README shows Settings.llm = Ollama(...) plus a HuggingFace embed model, which is the same interface, different implementation. Local stacks should also set Settings.tokenizer from the same tokenizer the model uses, so chunk budgets count tokens consistently across splitting and prompting. By default data lives in memory; index.storage_context.persist() writes it under ./storage for later reload.

The Ingestion Path: Documents to Nodes

The write path is where RAG quality is decided. Documents flow through a transformation list — typically the splitter first, then the embedder — each step reshaping nodes until they land in the store. There are two doors into this machinery: the one-liner VectorStoreIndex.from_documents used in the quickstart, and the standalone ingestion runner built with explicit transformations, a vector store and a docstore, which is what you graduate to once a corpus outgrows toy size. The runner also exposes num_workers, so large corpora can fan out across processes while the transformation list stays the same.

Three details matter. First, chunking is deterministic and inspectable: SentenceSplitter packs sentence boundaries against a token budget, so a chunk never ends mid-sentence unless a single sentence exceeds the budget. Second, re-ingesting does not mean re-embedding: IngestionCache keys intermediate results on the document hash, so an unchanged file skips every transformation on its second pass. Third, with a docstore attached, the runner can apply upsert-or-delete semantics, so updating one document replaces its stale nodes instead of appending duplicates — the failure mode that quietly poisons naive stores and makes retrieval return five near-identical stale chunks.

Retrieval: One Query Object, Many Stores

The read path starts with a translation problem: dozens of vector databases speak different dialects. LlamaIndex solves it with the VectorStoreQuery struct — embedding, top-k, query mode, metadata filters — and requires every provider to answer that one shape. SimpleVectorStore implements it with a dictionary and brute-force similarity, which makes the semantics easy to read; production stores implement the identical contract with HNSW trees and filtered scans — the same service you can also drive directly, as we showed in our Qdrant and pgvector source tours. Because the interface is uniform, swapping the backend is a constructor change, not a rewrite. Two more fields make the contract production-grade: filters carries structured metadata predicates so a store can prune before it ranks, and the hybrid fields (sparse_top_k, hybrid_top_k) let sparse and dense search share one call. That matters because a vector store is only as good as the recall/relevance trade you configure — something worth studying at the engine level before you let a framework abstract it away.

Response Synthesis Is Where the Tokens Go

Retrieval returns a list of NodeWithScore; the synthesizer decides how that becomes an answer, and the ResponseMode enum is really a menu of token economics. The default, COMPACT, is implemented by CompactAndRefine, whose _make_compact_text_chunks repacks the retrieved chunks so each LLM call is full rather than sending one small chunk per call — fewer calls, same context. TREE_SUMMARIZE goes the other way: TreeSummarize merges chunks in batches into partial summaries, then summarizes the summaries, trading extra calls for the ability to reason over far more retrieved text than any single prompt holds. REFINE iterates chunk by chunk, refining a rolling answer. The factory also accepts streaming and use_async flags, so the same strategy can stream tokens to a UI or run its LLM calls concurrently. Picking a mode is picking a latency/cost/quality trade-off, not a correctness knob — the same trade-off end-to-end RAG systems like RAGFlow expose through their own chunking and citation controls.

Agents Sit on Top, Not Inside

LlamaIndex’s agent layer is deliberately not in the query path. The core package’s llama_index.core.workflow namespace is a thin re-export of the external llama-index-workflows package (a pinned dependency in core’s pyproject.toml), which runs an event-driven loop: steps subscribe to events, StartEvent triggers execution, and agents like FunctionAgent are step graphs on that engine. The RAG machinery below stays a library — an agent can call a query engine as one tool among several, which keeps a single-document Q&A flow free of any loop machinery, and a multi-tool agent free of hardcoded retrieval. That separation is the sharpest contrast with LangChain, our previous tour, where the runnable-composition abstraction tends to absorb everything — models, tools, memory, retrieval — into one chain model. LlamaIndex instead composes at the data layer and leaves the control loop to a dedicated engine.

Honest Limits

Three caveats from reading the source. First, abstraction depth is real: a simple query crosses a query engine, retriever, store, synthesizer and callback manager, so stack traces grow long and debugging means learning all five layers — the price of the pluggability that makes providers swappable. Second, integration sprawl is real: with hundreds of provider packages, version skew between core and a provider is a routine failure mode, and the quickstart’s “pip install llama-index” hides many of these edges. Third, the defaults are sane but not magic: 1024-token chunks with 20 tokens of overlap is a reasonable starting point, not a tuning solution — the source makes the constants easy to find precisely because you are expected to change them. And like any fast-moving framework, the docs lag the code; the repository’s own README defers to a separate docs site whose pages trail API changes between releases. Treat documentation as orientation and the source as the contract — the tree in front of you is the truth.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of LlamaIndex: how documents become nodes, embeddings, vector-store hits and synthesized answers.

entry.title: PydanticAI Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Type-Safe Agents

link.title: PydanticAI Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Type-Safe Agents

entry.content:
Ask a typical agent framework to extract a structured record and it hands you a dictionary — whatever the model happened to emit, passed straight through. That is convenient right up until it is not: a missing field becomes a KeyError three functions away from the LLM call, a string 'true' masquerades as a boolean, and your type checker cannot warn you because, as far as it knows, the entire result is dict[str, Any]. In frameworks like LangChain or CrewAI, validation is something you bolt on after the fact, at every call site, forever.

PydanticAI — built by the team behind Pydantic itself — flips that default. The types are not decoration; they are the contract. Declare an output_type and every run is validated against it by the same core engine that validates your API payloads. Write tools as ordinary typed functions and their signatures become JSON Schema whose arguments are validated before your code executes. Dependencies arrive through a typed RunContext, so “give me the database handle” is solved with constructor-style typing instead of globals or string keys.

This post is a source tour of the GitHub main branch as of November 2026. Following a single agent.run_sync() call end to end reveals a small core: a pydantic-graph state machine with just a few node types that loops between model requests and tool dispatch until the output validates. The two diagrams below are generated from the real repository tree; the overview shows the moving parts, the detail map shows classes and line numbers. By the end you will know exactly where retries come from — and why each one costs a full extra model round-trip.

PydanticAI at a glance: your app talks to Agent, which runs a graph of request and tool-call nodes; models resolve through providers, results flow through message parts, output validation, and usage accounting.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Your application constructs Agent, L531 and calls run, run_sync, or iter — all inherited from AbstractAgent.run, L484 in the sibling abstract.py.
  • A run is literally a graph: build_agent_graph, L4893 wires nodes over GraphAgentState, L755 and GraphAgentDeps, L875 from the separate pydantic-graph package.
  • ModelRequestNode, L2263 turns history into parameters and calls the model — checking limits first via UsageLimits, L548.
  • The Model, L762 ABC is resolved from strings like openai:gpt-5 by infer_model, L2901; clients come from infer_provider, L432.
  • FallbackModel, L78 and InstrumentedModel, L466 are optional wrappers — failover and tracing — around whichever model you picked.
  • Every hop is a typed part in messages.py: ModelRequest, ModelResponse, ToolCallPart, ToolReturnPart.
  • CallToolsNode, L3784 dispatches tool calls to Tool, L355 objects, each carrying a ToolDefinition, L700 with the args schema.
  • Final output flows through OutputSchema, L553 and OutputValidator, L519 before becoming the FinalResult, L1236 you awaited.

The detail view: each box links to the source file. Note the two retry edges — one for failed tool arguments, one for failed output validation — both re-enter ModelRequestNode.

The Run Graph: Two Nodes in a Loop

PydanticAI does not hand-roll a while-loop; a run is a real state machine on the pydantic-graph engine. BaseNode, L33 subclasses each return the next node, and End, L62 terminates the run carrying the final result. The state and per-run dependencies travel in GraphRunContext, L24. If you have read our LangGraph internals tour, the shape is familiar — explicit nodes, explicit edges — except PydanticAI needs only a handful of node types because the domain is narrower.

Budget enforcement lives inside the loop, not around it. ModelRequestNode calls check_before_request before dispatching (L2977 and L3054) and re-checks after every response, accumulating RunUsage (L420) from per-call RequestUsage at L326. A run that exceeds its declared limits dies mid-graph with UsageLimitExceeded, L545 rather than completing with a warning.

The sequence: UserPromptNode, L1084 appends your prompt as a UserPromptPart, L1655 and loads instructions; ModelRequestNode.run, L2303 prepares parameters (the heavy lifting is in _prepare_request, L2901) and awaits the model. The response routes to CallToolsNode, L3784, which either executes tool calls and returns control to ModelRequestNode, or recognizes final output and hands it to SetFinalResult, L4307 before End. Streaming is the same loop with events: model_request_stream at L1989 feeds AgentStream, L58 and StreamedRunResult at L608. Where AutoGen drives a conversation between actors, PydanticAI’s loop is a function call cycle — arguably simpler to reason about, and the same philosophy CrewAI externalizes as tasks is compressed into one typed node.

How a Tool Call Becomes a Validated Function Call

A tool is an ordinary Python function wrapped by Tool, L355; the from_schema factory at L508 builds one from an explicit schema, while the @agent.tool decorator derives everything from the signature. The ToolDefinition, L700 dataclass is what the model actually sees: name, description, JSON Schema of the arguments, and flags like requires_approval.

At runtime process_tool_calls, L326 walks the response’s tool calls through processor classes (early, graceful, or exhaustive — L1204 onward) so error policy is pluggable. Arguments are parsed and validated against the schema before your function runs; if they fail, a RetryPromptPart, L2854 goes back to the model and each Tool honors its own max_retries (validated at L344). Successful results become a ToolReturnPart, L2711 appended to history. Tools can also arrive in bulk rather than one by one: anything implementing the toolset protocol — including MCPToolset, L776 for MCP servers — contributes tools through the same dispatch path, so the agent never special-cases where a tool came from. And the definition carries policy, not just shape: a tool flagged for human approval is serialized with kind unapproved (L577) so the model can be cut off before side effects happen. The first argument, when the function declares it, is RunContext, L224 — assembled per run by build_run_context at L4409 with your typed deps, live usage, and retry counters.

Output Modes and the Retry Loop

output_type accepts a plain Pydantic model or explicit mode markers in output.py: ToolOutput, L105 (answer via a tool call), NativeOutput, L182 (provider-native structured output), PromptedOutput, L239 (schema-in-prompt), TextOutput, L370, and StructuredDict at L401 for schemaless JSON. By default, the wrapper in OutputSchema, L553 resolves the mode and — in the tool mode — publishes the expected answer as an extra tool via OutputToolset, L1632, so “the model returns its answer” becomes “the model calls the answer into validation.”

That is the trick behind type safety: validation happens at a chokepoint. output_type may also be a union, in which case UnionOutputProcessor, L1256 wraps the alternatives in a synthetic model and validates whichever shape arrives; ToolOutputSchema at L887 handles fully manual schemas. OutputValidator, L519 instances run user checks, and on any ValidationError or ModelRetry, _make_retry_signal at L213 converts the failure into a retry rather than an exception. The retry is a message (RetryFeedbackPart, L2959) plus a fresh pass through ModelRequestNode — a real second API call. Only when validation passes does the output get wrapped in FinalResult, L1236 and returned as AgentRunResult, L938, usage included.

Providers, Profiles, and the Fallback Wrapper

The model layer is deliberately thin. A string like openai:gpt-5 is split by infer_model, L2901; the provider half goes through the Provider, L60 ABC and infer_provider, L432, which instantiates e.g. OpenAIProvider, L38 with the right SDK client. Per-model quirks — whether the vendor supports this feature, how tokens are counted — live in ModelProfile, L56, and request knobs like temperature live in ModelSettings, L130. Concrete chat models such as OpenAIChatModel, L1636 translate message parts into SDK calls.

Around any of these you can wrap behavior. FallbackModel, L78 implements request at L232 to try models in order on terminal failures. InstrumentedModel, L466 emits OpenTelemetry spans (configured via InstrumentationSettings at L83). TestModel, L62 answers deterministically for CI. MCP servers integrate as MCPToolset, L776 — they surface as ordinary toolsets to the same dispatch path. Usage accrues in RequestUsage/RunUsage (L326, L420) and is enforced by ModelRequestNode._enforce_usage_limits at L3743.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository README’s data-extraction example is the shortest honest demo. Install with uv add pydantic-ai (the core ships as the pydantic-ai-slim package, with optional extras per provider), then:

from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext


class Sentiment(BaseModel):
    label: Literal['positive', 'negative', 'neutral']
    score: float = Field(ge=-1, le=1)


agent = Agent('openai:gpt-6.1-sol', output_type=Sentiment)


@agent.tool
def recent_reviews(ctx: RunContext, product: str) -> list[str]:
    """Fetch recent review snippets for a product."""
    return ['The new release fixed everything I complained about!']


result = agent.run_sync('How are people feeling about the Extract app?')
print(result.output)
#> label='positive' score=0.9

Everything the tour explained is visible in eleven lines: the model string resolves through infer_model and infer_provider; the Sentiment output type becomes a validated contract; the recent_reviews signature and docstring become the tool schema; RunContext is where your dependencies would arrive; and result.output is a real Sentiment instance, not a dict — the README guarantees the run returns that type or an error, never raw text.

Honest Limits

  • Retries cost API calls. Every validation failure re-enters ModelRequestNode with retry feedback — a full extra round-trip per failure. Generous max_retries on flaky schemas can quietly multiply latency and spend.
  • The retry surface is mid-migration. RetryPromptPart is marked for removal — _output.py carries a TODO(v3): remove ... along with RetryPromptPart comment at L188 — in favor of RetryFeedbackPart. Older snippets using the legacy part will not survive v3 unchanged.
  • MCP naming has moved. The classic MCPServer classes are gone from this codebase; servers integrate as MCPToolset. Tutorials that predate the change will not match what you find here.
  • Cost limits can degrade to warnings. Token and request limits raise through UsageLimits.check_tokens at L681, but the enforcement path calls check_cost(..., warn_if_cost_unavailable=False) — when price data is missing, the run warns instead of failing.
  • Main moves fast. This tour is a snapshot of main as of 2026-11-08. The package has visibly restructured recently — there is no agent.py at the package root anymore (the class lives in the agent/ subpackage), so pinned line numbers and older blog snippets age quickly.
entry.summary: A source tour of PydanticAI: how Agent drives a two-node pydantic-graph run loop through ModelRequestNode and CallToolsNode to deliver schema-validated, typed outputs.

entry.title: BadgerDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Pure-Go LSM Key-Value Store

link.title: BadgerDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Pure-Go LSM Key-Value Store

entry.content:
Most storage engines we have toured in this series descend from the same C++ lineage: RocksDB and LevelDB pack keys and values into the same LSM tree and pay for it with compaction write amplification. BadgerDB, maintained by the Dgraph/Hypermode team, makes the opposite bet. It is an embeddable, persistent, pure-Go key-value store — no cgo, no C toolchain — built around the WiscKey paper (FAST ‘16), which separates keys from values so the LSM only ever carries tiny pointers. Badger is the storage engine underneath the Dgraph graph database, and it also powers Jaeger Tracing, so it is battle-tested on data sets the README describes as worth hundreds of terabytes.

Why should AI/ML infrastructure people care? Because Go increasingly hosts the serving side of ML systems: feature stores, agent state, session memory, and embedding caches live inside Go services where an embedded store beats a networked database by removing a hop.
