Badger’s key-value separation is especially friendly to that workload — large values like embedding vectors or serialized features are appended to an append-only value log, so compaction never rewrites them and reads of big values are fast sequential log reads. The README’s own comparison table highlights “high read throughput” and “pure Go (no cgo)” as deliberate design goals. If you want the graph-database connection, it is the same story as Neo4j: a purpose-built engine, except here the graph system (Dgraph) is layered on top of a general KV core. And if you want the Go-native LSM contrast from the transactional world, CockroachDB’s Pebble re-implements the classic design, while Badger re-thinks it.

In this tour we read the main branch of dgraph-io/badger (the v4 module line) from DB.Open to compaction, with two generated architecture diagrams. Everything cited below was verified against the actual source tree.

Overview: the write path flows from a client transaction through the oracle and a single write channel into the value log and memtable; flushing and compaction build SSTs that the read path merges back together.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup and state. Open, L195 replays the manifest, opens memtables and the value log, and starts flush and compaction goroutines. The DB struct, L82 holds the active memtable mt, immutable imm, the vlog, and the writeCh channel.
  • Transactions. NewTransaction, L757 pulls a read timestamp from the oracle, L24, the SSI authority that also tracks committed keys for conflict detection.
  • Commit. commitAndSend, L521 passes hasConflict, L128, gets a commit version from newCommitTs, L153, and hands entries to the write channel.
  • Value log first. writeRequests, L868 sends writes through vlog.write, L817; the LSM receives only a 16-byte-ish valuePointer, L15 of {fid, offset, len}.
  • Memtable. memTable.Put, L170 encodes a WAL record via logFile.encodeEntry, L283, then inserts into Skiplist.Put, L273, which bump-allocates nodes in an Arena, L26.
  • Flush. flushMemtable, L1151 drains full memtables into SSTs via Builder.Add, L332, then addLevel0Table, L1656 registers them in L0.
  • Compaction and metadata. doCompact, L1604 runs picked priorities through subcompact, L691 and compactBuildTables, L935, journaling results as a Manifest, L36 change set.
  • Reads. Txn.Get, L434 resolves to db.get, L789, which probes memtables then levelsController.get, L1721; scans use NewMergeIterator, L198 and missing values are fetched by valueLog.Read, L965.

Detail: each node is a grep-verified function or type in the badger source tree; follow the edges to see how a write becomes a memtable entry, an SST block, and finally a readable item.

WiscKey: Why the Value Log Exists

Badger’s defining idea is the WiscKey split. Classic LSM engines like RocksDB and LevelDB inline values into SSTs, so every compaction rewrites them — expensive when values are large. Badger appends values to append-only log files instead. The valueLog struct, L462 keeps a map of files and a head file for writes; vlog.write, L817 validates the batch, appends to the head file, and returns value pointers that the LSM stores in place of bytes. Only entries whose value exceeds ValueThreshold are spilled this way, and the default threshold is 1 MB (maxValueThreshold, options.go, L201), so in practice almost every meaningful value lives in the log. Files roll at roughly 1 GB (ValueLogFileSize, options.go, L165).

The cost of the split is garbage. Rewriting a log file to reclaim space is vlog.rewrite, L162, which streams live entries back into fresh files; users trigger it explicitly with RunValueLogGC, L1304 passing a discard ratio. There is also an adaptive vlogThreshold, L1138 that can tune the spill threshold from observed write sizes.

Durability defaults are tuned for throughput over latency: SyncWrites is false by default (options.go, L143), so callers needing a hard durability point call DB.Sync, L708, which syncs the memtable’s WAL and the value log. Every value-log record carries a CRC anyway, and the replay side (safeRead, L61) re-verifies it when entries are decoded back into memory.

The Write Path: SSI Transactions to Skiplist

Badger guarantees concurrent ACID transactions with serializable snapshot isolation, and the mechanism is compact enough to read in one sitting. oracle.readTs, L78 snapshots the world for a new transaction; oracle.hasConflict, L128 compares that snapshot against keys committed since; oracle.newCommitTs, L153 assigns the final version. Conflict detection is on by default (DetectConflicts: true, options.go, L175) and can be disabled per-database for read-mostly workloads.

Every key is physically versioned: KeyWithTs, L113 appends an 8-byte timestamp to the user key, ParseTs, L121 peels it back, and CompareKeys, L132 orders by key first, version descending. That is why a “3D access (key-value-version)” row appears in the README comparison table — iterators can walk all versions of a key.

Backpressure is explicit. ensureRoomForWrite, L1044 blocks writes when too many memtables or L0 tables pile up: defaults are NumMemtables: 5, NumLevelZeroTables: 5, and stall at NumLevelZeroTablesStall: 15 (options.go, L128-140). Progress accounting runs through the generic WaterMark, L51, whose WaitForMark, L104 lets goroutines wait until all earlier work has finished — the same primitive backs transaction and compaction sequencing. The Throttle, L187 in y gates in-flight batches. One detail worth noting: the commit path batches aggressively. doWrites, L943 coalesces whatever requests have piled up in the channel and writes them out together, so hundreds of small transactions can share a single value-log append and a single memtable fill — one of the reasons Badger sustains very high write throughput in the benchmarks the README links.

SST Format: Blocks, Flatbuffer Index, Bloom Filters

The SST builder (Builder, L68) accumulates 4 KB blocks (BlockSize, default in DefaultOptions, L123), prefix-compresses keys against their predecessor, and closes a block in finishBlock, L262 when shouldFinishBlock says so. Per-block CRCs guard against silent corruption. buildIndex, L526 then serializes block offsets, key counts, and max versions as a flatbuffer (the generated Go lives in fb/), followed by a bloom filter built with NewFilter, L45 at a false-positive rate of 0.01. On read, DoesNotHave, L699 rejects tables cheaply before any block is touched.

Reading an SST is mmap-first: OpenTable, L268 memory-maps the file and parses the index, while Table.block, L552 fetches cached blocks (a 256 MB block cache is the default) and binary-searches them with the blockIterator, L18. Range scans stack per-level iterators into the heap-based merge iterator, and the DB-level machinery that stitches memtables plus levels together lives in appendIterators, L1768. Because tables inside levels below L0 do not overlap, scans fold each level’s tables into one ConcatIterator, L426 that steps through them in key order (the L1+ branch of appendIterators, L365). Point lookups take a cheaper route: bloom check first, then a per-table iterator Seek (level_handler.go, L308). If you are paranoid about bit rot, VerifyChecksum, L698 re-hashes every block of every table on demand.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps setup minimal, and it matches what we verified in the tree. Badger v3+ requires Go 1.23 or above and go modules; from your project run go get github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4, which fetches the library as an embedded dependency. For offline maintenance tooling (backup, restore, flatten, info), the README shows installing the CLI from the repository’s badger subdirectory with cd badger followed by go install ., which drops a badger binary into your $GOBIN.

A minimal feature-record write, using only API surface we verified above, looks like this:

import badger "github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4"

db, err := badger.Open(badger.DefaultOptions("/tmp/feature-store"))
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer db.Close()

txn := db.NewTransaction(true) // read-write; gets readTs from the oracle
if err := txn.Set([]byte("emb:user:42"), vectorBytes); err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := txn.Commit(); err != nil {
    return err
}

DefaultOptions is a good starting point: 64 MB memtables, snappy compression, and a 256 MB block cache. For bulk loads, prefer the write batch API (NewWriteBatch, L39, flushed with WriteBatch.Flush, L211); for online model training loops that read at fixed versions, managed mode’s NewTransactionAt, L23 pins a snapshot. Large parallel dumps and restores can use the streaming interfaces (Stream.Orchestrate, L415 and StreamWriter.Flush, L252), which fan work across goroutines.

Honest Limits

Badger is a KV library, not a database server. There is no SQL layer, no secondary indexes, and no query language — you get Get, Set, Delete, iteration, and versions; anything richer you build yourself (or take from Dgraph, BadgerHold, and friends). It is embedded and single-node: there is no built-in network protocol or replication, so high availability is your job, typically via raft-backed wrappers. There is a pure in-memory mode (an InMemory option gates all value-log and file I/O, as seen at value.go, L818), handy for ephemeral caches and tests, but it is still a library, not a service.

Operationally, the WiscKey trade cuts both ways. Value-log garbage needs periodic, explicit GC (RunValueLogGC, L1304), and picking the discard ratio is a judgment call. The tuning surface is large — Options, L31 exposes dozens of knobs from MemTableSize to NumCompactors: 4 and MaxLevels: 7 — and wrong settings show up as stalls rather than errors. Versioned keys mean a naive iterator can see multiple versions per key unless NumVersionsToKeep and iterator options are set deliberately. Finally, the README’s platform table notes real caveats: directory fsync is unsupported on AIX, file locking differs on Windows, and Plan9/WASM lack locking — worth reading dir_*.go before unusual deployments. Documentation is serviceable but thin (the in-repo docs/ folder plus badger.dgraph.io), so the source, as always, is the real manual — much easier to read here than in C++, and a good companion to Pebble if you are comparing Go LSM designs.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of BadgerDB, the pure-Go WiscKey-based LSM key-value store behind Dgraph, covering transactions, skiplist memtables, the value log, compaction, and the manifest.

entry.title: CockroachDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine Built to Survive Anything

link.title: CockroachDB Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Distributed SQL Engine Built to Survive Anything

entry.content:
If you are serving AI features to users in several regions at once, you eventually hit the same wall: a single-node Postgres works beautifully until you need writes to survive a datacenter failure, or until feature data, embeddings metadata, and audit trails have to stay transactionally consistent across continents. CockroachDB is the open-source answer that industry keeps reaching for — a distributed SQL database written in Go that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, scales horizontally by splitting data into replicated ranges, and refuses to lose an acknowledged write even when machines are failing underneath it. For ML platforms specifically, it is a natural backing store for regional feature stores, vector-metadata joins, and anything where a stale or lost row quietly corrupts a model’s inputs.

What makes it fascinating to read at the source level is how little magic there is. Everything reduces to one repeated loop: a SQL statement becomes a transactional batch of key-value requests, that batch is routed to a leaseholder replica, the replica evaluates it against multi-version MVCC state, the result is replicated through Raft, and the whole thing rests on an LSM-tree engine called Pebble. If you have followed our earlier storage-engine tours of RocksDB and LevelDB, you will feel at home immediately — Pebble is the direct Go descendant of that same LSM lineage, purpose-built by Cockroach Labs when they outgrew embedding RocksDB as a C++ library inside their Go process.

In this tour we read the actual code in the cockroachdb/cockroach monorepo and draw two architecture diagrams from it: an overview of the full query path, and a detailed map of the functions that make it work. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the current master branch, so the links drop you straight into the source.

Overview: one query's journey from a Postgres-compatible socket to replicated LSM storage. Every edge is a real call path in the Go source.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A session is just a wire protocol. The pgwire conn struct (conn, L59) accepts the same PostgreSQL frontend/backend protocol that Postgres speaks, so existing drivers connect with zero code changes. Server.ServeConn (ServeConn, L991) upgrades each connection into a SQL session.
  • Sessions run a state machine. connExecutor (connExecutor, L1609) owns transaction state, and execStmt (execStmt, L123) with execStmtInOpenState (execStmtInOpenState, L417) drive every statement through it.
  • Every query is optimized, not interpreted. planner.makeOptimizerPlan (makeOptimizerPlan, L298) builds a memo of alternative plans and prices them; coster.ComputeCost (coster.ComputeCost, L526) is where join orders and index choices actually get decided.
  • Plans become physical flows. The PhysicalPlan (PhysicalPlan, L125) assigns operators to nodes, and flows of ProcessorBase instances (ProcessorBase, L345) execute them locally or distributed.
  • SQL touches data only through KV. Row sources end up in Txn.Send (Txn.Send, L1386), which funnels batches into the TxnCoordSender (TxnCoordSender, L510) for intent tracking and retries.
  • Batches are routed, not broadcast. DistSender.Send (DistSender.Send, L1310) splits a BatchRequest by key range and sendToReplicas (sendToReplicas, L2669) targets each range’s leaseholder replica over gRPC.
  • One Node fronts one process. Inbound RPCs land in Node.batchInternal (batchInternal, L1648), which hands work to the Store (Store, L909) that owns replicas on local disks.
  • Replicas evaluate, then replicate. The Replica (Replica, L365) evaluates the batch under its lease, and evalAndPropose (evalAndPropose, L116) proposes the result to Raft so a majority durably agrees.
  • Everything ends in Pebble. The Pebble engine (Pebble, L884) implements the Engine interface (Engine, L932) and persists both the Raft log and the MVCC keyspace.

The detailed map: 34 components from wire protocol to LSM compactions, with the exact functions that glue each layer to the next.

SQL: From Wire Protocol to Costed Memo

The SQL layer’s discipline is striking: there is exactly one optimizer, and nothing bypasses it. optbuilder.Builder.Build (Builder.Build, L263) converts the parsed AST into a memo — a DAG of relational expressions where equivalent alternatives share groups. The xform explorer then applies transformation rules via exploreGroup (exploreGroup, L155) until the Coster (coster.ComputeCost, L526) can no longer find a cheaper expression. Cost here is not an abstract score: it is calibrated in units of IO, CPU, and memory (the Cost type lives in Cost, L17), which is why the optimizer can reason sensibly about wide scans of embedding tables versus narrow index lookups on feature keys.

Execution follows the same decomposition. dispatchToExecutionEngine (dispatchToExecutionEngine, L2887) picks between local and distributed plans, execWithDistSQLEngine (execWithDistSQLEngine, L3664) sets up flows, and each node runs its fragment through the Flow interface (Flow, L72). Processors stream rows to each other rather than materializing whole tables — the same pull-based style that makes DuckDB-class engines cache-friendly.

KV: TxnCoordSender and the DistSender

Beneath SQL, CockroachDB is a transactional key-value store, and the client side of that store is small enough to hold in your head. kv.DB (DB, L272) hands out Txn handles; batches stage operations like Batch.Put (Batch.Put, L460) as kvpb requests. The TxnCoordSender (TxnCoordSender, L510) is the transaction’s brain: it records which ranges hold intents, heartbeats the transaction record so other nodes can tell a live writer from a crashed one, and orchestrates retries.

The DistSender (DistSender, L726) then does geography: it consults the range metadata to find which leaseholder serves each key span, splits the batch accordingly, and re-runs pieces when ranges split or leaders move mid-flight. By default every transaction runs at SERIALIZABLE isolation — the strongest level Postgres only offers opt-in — implemented through MVCC timestamps and read refreshes rather than lock tables.

Replication: Ranges, Leases, and Raft

Each range (a contiguous key span, default 512 MiB) is owned by a Replica on each of its three or more voting stores. Exactly one replica holds the lease at a time; pendingLeaseRequest.requestLease (requestLease, L552) and its async variant (requestLeaseAsync, L474) make acquisition cooperative and liveness-aware. Only the leaseholder may serve consistent reads, which is why the diagram routes every batch through it.

Writes then follow classic Raft. evaluateBatch (evaluateBatch, L198) runs the batch against current state to produce a result; evalAndPropose (evalAndPropose, L116) turns that into a proposed command with a MaxLeaseIndex for replay protection; propose (propose, L411) enqueues it; and handleRaftReady (handleRaftReady, L867) drains the ready data into the log and transport. The consensus algorithm itself lives in the vendored pkg/raft library (raft, L305), a heavily-evolved descendant of etcd’s raft. Acknowledgment waits for a majority, so a range survives losing a minority of its replicas with no human intervention.

Storage: MVCC over a Pebble LSM

The storage engine contract is the Engine interface (Engine, L932) — a versioned reader/writer — and Pebble is its production implementation (Pebble, L884). MVCC keys are literally user keys suffixed with wall-clock timestamps, so MVCCGet (MVCCGet, L1401) and MVCCPut (MVCCPut, L1923) are LSM operations over that encoding, with mvccPutInternal (mvccPutInternal, L2251) deciding between values and tombstoned intents. Scans merge intents and versions through pebbleMVCCScanner (pebbleMVCCScanner, L381).

This is the part of the codebase our series has been circling for months: Pebble takes the LSM ideas RocksDB refined from LevelDB — memtables, tiered SSTables, bloom filters, compactions — and re-implements them in pure Go, adding level-aware write amplification control that suits CockroachDB’s raft-append-heavy workload. Reading pkg/storage right after those two codebases is a genuinely satisfying experience.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything below comes straight from the repository’s own README. The quickest route is a pre-built binary: the README’s “Starting with CockroachDB” list points at the documented installer page for your platform. If you would rather build from source, the README’s “Building from source” section defers to the project wiki; expect a Bazel-driven build — the repo’s GNUmakefile is a thin wrapper whose build target just runs ./dev build, and ./dev in turn drives Bazel. Budget real time and disk for the first compile; this is a large monorepo with C dependencies.

Once you have a cockroach binary: start a local demo cluster with three nodes as the README suggests, open the built-in SQL client, create a database and table, and then connect your application with any PostgreSQL driver or ORM — the README explicitly notes that the PostgreSQL wire protocol is supported, so psycopg2, asyncpg, or SQLAlchemy all work unchanged. For an ML service, your first schema might be a features table keyed by entity ID with an _updated_at column, giving you transactional feature reads alongside the labels you train on.

Honest Limits

Read the license before you plan around it. Since the v24.3 series (releases after November 18, 2024, per the README’s licensing section), the code ships under the CockroachDB Software License rather than an OSI-approved open-source license: the LICENSE file grants use and modification for operating, testing, and improving CockroachDB, but prohibits offering it as a commercial DBaaS without a license key. Source-available, yes; fully open-source, no. For an internal AI platform this is usually irrelevant, but check it before embedding.

Engineering costs are real, too. The monorepo is enormous (over 20,000 tracked files), builds run through Bazel with a custom ./dev tool, and running a production cluster means operating at least three nodes, monitoring Raft health, and accepting that every write pays a consensus round-trip. It is a server, not an embeddable library — there is no “just link it into your app” mode like SQLite’s. For single-region workloads that fit in one machine, plain Postgres remains simpler; for battery-backup-grade regional consistency, that trade is exactly what you are buying.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of CockroachDB's Go monorepo, tracing a query from the PostgreSQL wire protocol through the cost-based optimizer, the DistSender, Raft replication, and down into the Pebble LSM storage engine.

entry.title: Dolt Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Git for Data

link.title: Dolt Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Git for Data

entry.content:
Every serious ML effort eventually collides with the same question: which exact rows did this model train on? Training data is not static. Labels get corrected, schemas grow columns, bad batches are rolled back, and feature-engineering experiments fork the dataset in different directions. File-based snapshots — folders of CSV or Parquet dumps — cannot answer lineage questions cleanly, and homegrown version columns rot fast. Dolt takes the radically honest approach: it is a real SQL database where every data revision is a commit, and the whole toolbox you know from Git — clone, branch, merge, diff, push, pull — applies to tables. Where table-format projects such as Apache Iceberg version files and snapshots in object storage, Dolt versions the rows themselves, inside a transactional SQL engine, down to per-cell history queries.

The practical hook is compatibility. Dolt speaks the MySQL wire protocol, so existing clients, connectors and BI tools attach to it like any MySQL server, while version control shows up as SQL system tables (dolt_log, dolt_status, dolt_diff_<table>) and stored procedures (dolt_add, dolt_commit, dolt_merge). The project’s own README compresses the idea into one line: “Git versions files. Dolt versions tables.” For ML teams this means dataset audits, branch-and-merge feature experiments, and push/pull collaboration with the operational model of Git but the query power of SQL — no new export formats, no sidecar metadata store.

In this tour we read the actual source of dolthub/dolt on the main branch (verified at commit f16514116453), walking from the MySQL entry points down to the chunk store, then zooming into the mechanics that make versioned tables fast: Prolly Trees, content addressing, and the commit machinery. Every symbol below was checked against the tree at that commit.

Overview: queries enter through the CLI or the MySQL-compatible server, flow through the SQL engine and version core, and land as rows in Prolly Trees whose chunks are persisted by the Noms block store alongside commit objects.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SqlCmd, L114 implements dolt sql, the interactive shell and one-off query mode that ships inside the single binary.
  • SqlServerCmd, L162 starts the MySQL-wire-compatible server, so any MySQL client can connect without knowing versioning exists.
  • DoltSession, L50 carries per-connection state — current database, branch, transaction — bridging SQL sessions onto version control.
  • RootValue, L59 is the immutable snapshot interface: table names resolved to table values, the object every query reads and every commit pins.
  • DoltDB, L128 is the version-control facade; its Resolve, L532 turns a CommitSpec like HEAD~ into a concrete commit.
  • Map (prolly.Map), L32 is the Prolly Tree map holding encoded row tuples, with Get, L264 for point lookups.
  • Node, L40 and the NodeStore, L38 interface manage the immutable tree nodes that give Prolly Trees their structural sharing.
  • ChunkStore, L74 is the content-addressed persistence contract, implemented on disk by NomsBlockStore, L97.
  • Dataset, L468 models refs — branches and working sets — whose heads point at commit objects, the final layer of the stack.

Detail: CLI verbs map onto staging and commit actions; the engine reads roots and prolly-backed indexes; mutations flush through the tree mutator into chunks, the manifest, the journal and table files.

Prolly Trees: Chunks With Structural Sharing

The storage story starts at the bottom. A Chunk, L33 is simply a byte slice plus its content hash — Dolt inherits this unit from the Noms project it credits in its README. Hashes are fixed-size Hash, L80 values, so every object in the system is addressed by the cryptographic digest of its content. Writes never mutate existing chunks; new content means new chunks with new addresses.

Prolly Trees are the clever part. A Node, L40 is an immutable tree node whose leaves hold key/value tuples, and node boundaries are chosen probabilistically from content — which is what makes the tree “prolly” (probabilistic B-tree). When you edit a map you do not touch it directly: Mutate, L216 hands you a MutableMap, L54 (an alias for the generic GenericMutableMap) that accumulates edits, with Put, L123 and delete operations buffered before flush. Flushing runs ApplyMutations, L63, which rewrites only the paths of the tree that changed, serializing each new node through NewProllyMapSerializer, L43. Because interior nodes address their children by hash, unchanged subtrees are physically shared between any two versions of the map.

That single design decision is why Dolt can diff, merge and time-travel cheaply. Two commits differ exactly in the chunks that differ, and merges reuse the common ancestor’s shared nodes. It is a different trade-off from the LSM engines of RocksDB, which optimize for write amplification on mutable data; Dolt optimizes for cheap immutable versions of mutable data.

Commits, Refs and the Version Core

Above storage sits the Git-like object model. The string you type — HEAD~, a branch name, a commit hash — is parsed by NewCommitSpec, L97 into a CommitSpec, L64; the ~ and ^ suffixes are split off by SplitAncestorSpec, L109 into an AncestorSpec, L80. Resolve, L532 then walks refs to produce a Commit, L49 — the familiar trio of parent hashes, a root pointer, and metadata.

The working-copy model maps cleanly onto tables. WorkingSet, L316 holds the working, staged and head roots for a branch. dolt add triggers StageTables, L26, copying table roots from the working root to the staged root; dolt commit goes through GetCommitStaged, L80, which validates constraints and builds the commit with NewCommitMeta, L129 capturing author, email and message. Refs themselves are Dataset, L468 values managed by the Database, L51 layer, and CommitValue, L568 atomically swaps a head to the new commit. History queries such as dolt_log read back metadata with GetCommitMeta, L428.

The SQL Surface: Sessions, Indexes and the Wire

The engine integration is where Dolt stops feeling like Git bolted onto a database. DoltSession, L50 binds each connection to a database session state, and the adapter in go/libraries/doltcore/sqle/database.go exposes dolt databases to the GMS SQL analyzer so standard queries, joins and transactions behave as you expect. Secondary indexes are Prolly Trees too — index scans run through prollyIndexIter, L34, and table structure is described by the Schema, L43 interface of columns, primary keys and index collections.

The wire path matters for ML workflows because it is how Python reaches the data: SqlServerCmd, L162 starts the server, and from there a plain mysql client or any MySQL driver can query dolt_history_<table> for row-level lineage. We compared the MySQL server codebase itself in our MySQL source tour; Dolt’s approach is the opposite end — reimplementing the protocol surface natively in Go rather than carrying the C++ server.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps onboarding deliberately boring, which is a feature. Install the single binary — roughly 103 MB — via the release install script for Linux/macOS, brew install dolt on Mac, the .msi or choco install dolt on Windows, or build from source inside the repo’s go directory with go install ./cmd/dolt (Go plus a C toolchain, since Dolt depends on cgo). Configure your identity exactly like Git: dolt config --global --add user.email you@domain.com and the matching user.name.

Then create your first versioned dataset:

mkdir ml-datasets && cd ml-datasets
dolt init
dolt sql -q "create table training_runs (id int primary key, model varchar(255), row_count int)"
dolt add training_runs
dolt commit -m "initial training_runs schema"

dolt init creates the empty data repository, dolt sql -q runs one query and exits, and add/commit stage and record table changes. From Python you can connect with any MySQL library, run inserts between training epochs, and commit checkpoints — every snapshot of the dataset is now addressable. The README also shows the SQL-procedure equivalents for server-side use: call dolt_add('training_runs') and call dolt_commit('-m', 'message'), with dolt_log, dolt_status and dolt_diff_<table> as inspection points. Branches work identically: call dolt_checkout('-b', 'feature-experiment'), mutate and commit, then call dolt_merge('feature-experiment') back into main — the README’s walkthrough demonstrates the full round trip, including as of time-travel queries against a branch.

Honest Limits

Dolt’s compatibility claim deserves precision. The README recommends MySQL clients up to version 8.4 and notes that MySQL 9.0’s caching_sha2_password authentication needs extra configuration to connect; the server also identifies itself as 5.7.9-Vitess, a nod to the Vitess-derived SQL engine, so scripts that sniff server versions can be surprised. Compatibility is broad — foreign keys, secondary indexes, triggers, checks and stored procedures are supported per the README — but it is not bit-for-bit MySQL parity.

The versioning superpowers are not free. Content addressing and structural sharing add bookkeeping that a plain B-tree engine serving purely mutable OLTP data does not pay, and the write path funnels through chunk flushes rather than in-place page updates. The distribution model has its own footprint: one Go binary of about 103 MB, a large Go monorepo (several thousand files at HEAD), and a cgo dependency for building from source. If your dialect is Postgres rather than MySQL, the README points to the separate Doltgres project, which is in Beta. None of these are disqualifiers for the dataset-versioning niche; they are the price of putting Git semantics inside a transactional SQL engine.

What to Steal for Your Own Stack

Three ideas transfer well beyond Dolt. First, content addressing as the substrate: if every object’s name is its hash, diffing, deduplication and integrity checks fall out of the design for free — the same insight behind LevelDB-style immutable table files, here taken to the whole database. Second, structural sharing: probabilistic node splitting is what turns “store every snapshot” from wasteful to nearly free, a technique any snapshot-heavy system can borrow. Third, the session-root design: keeping working, staged and head roots per branch (WorkingSet, L316) is a clean pattern for any system that needs drafts, staging and published state as first-class data. Dolt is the rare database whose source reads like an argument that version control is a storage-engine property, not a bolt-on feature — and for ML data workflows, that argument lands.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of dolthub/dolt, the MySQL-compatible SQL database that versions tables with content-addressed Prolly Trees, commits, branches and merges.
